solution.concept_anchor: UPSC historical evolution from Federal Public Service Commission
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students familiar with the 1919 Government of India Act often associate early civil service reform with that period, making 1919 feel plausible.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Federal Public Service Commission was not established in 1919; the year 1919 relates to the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms.
Eliminate option (c): 1935 is associated with the Government of India Act, not the establishment of the Federal Public Service Commission.
Eliminate option (d): 1947 is the year of Independence, not the year of this body's establishment.
Confirm option (b): The Federal Public Service Commission was established in 1926 under the Lee Commission recommendations, which later became UPSC in 1950.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently confuse the constitutional reform milestones — 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford) and 1935 (GoI Act) — with the administrative milestones like the Lee Commission of 1923–24 that recommended an independent public service commission, established in 1926. The trap exploits the clustering of dates around major legislative acts.
solution.final_explanation:
The Union Public Service Commission traces its lineage to the Federal Public Service Commission established in 1926, based on the recommendations of the Lee Commission (1923–24). This body was reconstituted as the UPSC upon the Constitution's commencement in 1950 under Articles 315–323 (Part XIV).

• Option (a) — 1919: Incorrect. This year marks the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms and the Government of India Act, 1919 — not the civil service commission.
• Option (b) — 1926: Correct. The Federal Public Service Commission was formally established in 1926.
• Option (c) — 1935: Incorrect. The Government of India Act, 1935 reorganised federal structures but was not the founding year of the commission.
• Option (d) — 1947: Incorrect. This is the year of Independence, not the commission's founding.

Value Addition:
• The Lee Commission's full name was the Royal Commission on Superior Civil Services in India.
• UPSC is governed by Articles 315–323 under Part XIV ('Services Under the Union and the States').
• The UPSC was the first constitutional body to be constituted after the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 316 — no fixed membership strength prescribed

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution prescribes a fixed number of members for the Union Public Service Commission.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 316 leaves the determination of the number of UPSC members entirely to the President — no fixed number is mentioned in the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: The Constitution prescribes no minimum educational or professional qualification for appointment as a member of the UPSC.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution contains no qualification criteria for UPSC members; the only mandatory condition relates to prior government service experience for at least half the members.

statement_analysis.statement: At least half of the members of the UPSC must have held office under the Government of India or a State Government for a minimum of ten years at the time of appointment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 316(2) mandates that not less than one-half of the members must have been in government service for at least ten years prior to appointment.

solution.strong_distractor: b — A student recalling that 'half the members must have experience' might wrongly select only statement 3 as correct, forgetting that statement 1 is the one that is incorrect.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: The Constitution gives the President the discretion to determine UPSC strength — no fixed number is prescribed anywhere in Articles 315–323.
Statement 2 is correct: Unlike the judiciary or CAG, no educational qualification is mandated for UPSC membership.
Statement 3 is correct: Article 316 explicitly requires at least half the members to have ten years of government service.
Correct combination is statements 2 and 3 only — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Many students assume that a constitutional body of UPSC's importance must have prescribed qualifications and fixed membership strength — analogising it with the Supreme Court (fixed by Parliament) or constitutional posts requiring specific qualifications. This question exploits both misconceptions simultaneously.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 316 governs the composition of UPSC. The President determines the number of members — the Constitution itself fixes no number. This is a deliberate design to allow flexibility. No educational or professional qualification is prescribed; the only structural condition is that at least half the members must have a minimum of ten years of government service.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The President determines UPSC strength; no fixed number appears in the Constitution.
• Statement 2 — Correct: There is a complete absence of prescribed qualifications — unlike High Court judges who must be advocates of ten years standing.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 316(2) mandates the 'at least half with ten-year government service' condition.

Value Addition:
• UPSC currently has a Chairman and ten members by convention, though this is not constitutionally mandated.
• The ten-year service condition applies at the time of appointment — not at any subsequent point.
• This flexibility contrasts with the Election Commission, where the Supreme Court has read in certain structural protections.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC vs SPSC retirement age — 65 vs 62

statement_analysis.statement: Members of both the UPSC and State Public Service Commissions retire at the age of 65.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC members retire at 65, but State PSC members retire at 62 — a key constitutional distinction under Article 316(2) and its state PSC equivalent.

statement_analysis.statement: A member of the UPSC who has completed a full term is not eligible for reappointment to the same commission.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 316(3) bars a UPSC member who has completed a full term from reappointment to the UPSC.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairman of the UPSC, after vacating office, is ineligible for any further employment under the Government of India or any State Government.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution imposes a post-retirement bar on the UPSC Chairman from all further government employment, ensuring independence during tenure.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Many students who know that UPSC members retire at 65 assume (incorrectly) that the same age applies to State PSC members, making statement 1 appear correct when it is not.
elimination_logic: Statement 2 is factually correct: reappointment bar after full term is established under Article 316.
Statement 3 is factually correct: the post-retirement bar on UPSC Chairman is explicit in the Constitution.
Statement 1 is factually incorrect: SPSC members retire at 62, not 65 — making it the NOT correct statement.
Since only statement 1 is incorrect, the answer is option (a) — 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The retirement age difference (UPSC at 65; SPSC at 62) is one of the most frequently tested and most frequently confused distinctions in UPSC Prelims. Students who know only UPSC's age limit of 65 extend it to State PSCs by analogy, which is wrong. This question places that false statement alongside two correct statements to isolate whether the student knows the precise constitutional distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 316(2) fixes the tenure of UPSC members at six years or age 65, whichever is earlier. For State PSC members, the corresponding age is 62 — a deliberate constitutional difference that is heavily tested.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: SPSC members retire at 62, not 65. The 65-year limit applies only to UPSC members.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A UPSC member who completes a full six-year term cannot be reappointed to the same position.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The UPSC Chairman faces an absolute post-retirement bar from any government employment, unlike ordinary members who may be appointed to other constitutional posts.

Value Addition:
• A UPSC member (not Chairman) can be appointed as Chairman of UPSC or as Chairman/member of an SPSC after retirement.
• An SPSC Chairman can be appointed to UPSC or another SPSC after vacating office — mobility is allowed except for the UPSC Chairman.
• The 62-year limit for SPSC mirrors the retirement age of High Court judges for mnemonic purposes.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 317 — five grounds for UPSC member removal

statement_analysis.statement: A UPSC member has been adjudicated insolvent.
statement_analysis.reason: Insolvency is one of the five specified grounds under Article 317(1) for removal of a UPSC member.

statement_analysis.statement: A UPSC member has engaged in paid employment outside the duties of her office.
statement_analysis.reason: Engagement in paid activities outside official duties is an explicit ground for removal under Article 317.

statement_analysis.statement: A UPSC member has publicly criticised a government recruitment policy.
statement_analysis.reason: Public criticism of policy is not among the five specified grounds; the Constitution lists only insolvency, outside paid employment, infirmity of mind or body, misbehaviour, and engagement in prejudicial activities.

statement_analysis.statement: A UPSC member has been found to have interests prejudicial to the functions of the office.
statement_analysis.reason: Having interests prejudicial to the commission's functions — linked to the misbehaviour ground — is a constitutionally specified basis for removal.

solution.strong_distractor: c — A student who knows three grounds clearly may count three as the answer but overlook that statement 3 is not a constitutional ground, leading them to choose 'Only three.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is a valid ground: insolvency is explicitly listed in Article 317(1).
Statement 2 is a valid ground: engagement in paid outside employment is explicitly listed.
Statement 3 is NOT a valid constitutional ground: public policy criticism is not among the five enumerated grounds.
Statement 4 is a valid ground: prejudicial interests / misbehaviour is listed.

Three out of four statements describe valid grounds — answer is option (b) Only two... wait — recounting: statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct grounds; statement 3 is not. That is three correct, so answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The five grounds for UPSC member removal are specific and exhaustive — students who study them broadly may include plausible-sounding additions like 'public criticism' or 'contempt of Parliament.' Statement 3 exploits this by inserting a democratic-sounding but constitutionally absent ground, tempting students who are uncertain about the exact list.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 317(1) specifies the grounds on which the President may remove a UPSC member. These grounds are exhaustive, not illustrative. The five grounds are: (i) adjudged insolvent, (ii) engagement in paid employment outside official duties, (iii) infirmity of mind or body, (iv) misbehaviour, and (v) interests prejudicial to the functions of the commission. Importantly, removal on the ground of misbehaviour requires a mandatory Supreme Court inquiry.

• Statement 1 — Valid ground: insolvency explicitly listed.
• Statement 2 — Valid ground: paid outside employment explicitly listed.
• Statement 3 — NOT a valid ground: public criticism of government policy does not appear among the five constitutional grounds — it is a plausible fabrication.
• Statement 4 — Valid ground: prejudicial interests/misbehaviour is listed.

Three statements (1, 2, 4) describe valid grounds.

Value Addition:
• The President can suspend a UPSC member pending a Supreme Court inquiry.
• The Supreme Court's inquiry under Article 317 results in a recommendation — the President is bound by it.
• This removal procedure mirrors that of CAG and Election Commissioners, placing UPSC in the same independence tier.
solution.correct_option_note: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct grounds — three out of four — answer is (c) Only three.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional safeguards for UPSC independence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps the constitutional provision for service condition protection (Article 318) with Article 317, which students who know Article 317 deals with removal may accept without checking Article 318.
elimination_logic: Article 317 deals with removal and suspension — it matches with 'Removal requires Supreme Court inquiry' (D-3).
Article 318 deals with regulations for service conditions — it matches with 'Service conditions cannot be varied to disadvantage after appointment' (B-1).
Charged on Consolidated Fund of India means Parliament cannot vote on UPSC budget — matches C-4.
Post-retirement employment bar applies to the UPSC Chairman specifically — matches A-2.
Full matching: A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3 — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap works by mixing Article 317 (removal) and Article 318 (service conditions) — two adjacent articles that students often blur. A partially prepared student who associates 'independence safeguards' primarily with removal (Article 317) may misattribute the service conditions protection to the same article.
solution.final_explanation:
The Constitution embeds multiple safeguards for UPSC independence across different articles. Article 318 empowers the President to frame regulations but simultaneously bars variation of service conditions to the disadvantage of members after appointment. The Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) route for UPSC expenditure insulates it from Parliamentary budget cuts. The post-retirement employment bar on the Chairman prevents anticipatory obedience. Article 317 ensures that even the removal power is checked by a mandatory Supreme Court inquiry.

Correct matching:
• A (Post-retirement bar on Chairman) → 2 (Freedom from executive influence during tenure)
• B (Service conditions fixed after appointment) → 1 (Article 318 protection)
• C (Expenditure on CFI) → 4 (Insulation from Parliamentary vote)
• D (Removal through SC inquiry) → 3 (Article 317 quasi-judicial check)

Trap pairings: Students may link D (removal) to Article 318 or confuse B with Article 317.

Value Addition:
• The CAG, CEC, and UPSC members share the 'charged on CFI' feature — a key grouping for exam purposes.
• Article 310 (doctrine of pleasure) is explicitly overridden for UPSC members by Article 317.
• No Parliamentary resolution is needed to remove a UPSC member — unlike judges (who require an address by Parliament).

Obligatory vs. Discretionary Consultation with UPSC

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC consultation mandatory but advice not binding
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts — mandatory consultation and executive discretion — may assume the latter follows from the former causally, selecting (a) without recognising that these are two independent constitutional design choices.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Constitution under Article 320(3) mandates consultation with UPSC on enumerated matters; this is obligatory, not optional.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. Failure to consult UPSC does NOT invalidate the action taken — Supreme Court has confirmed this. The Reason misstates the legal consequence.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer maps to option (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: option (c) — A correct, R incorrect — matches correct_option.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits a common conflation between 'mandatory consultation' and 'mandatory compliance.' Students know consultation is compulsory and reason that non-compliance must therefore invalidate the act — but the Supreme Court has held otherwise. The Reason sounds like a logical consequence of the Assertion, making it a classic reversed-causation trap.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional design of UPSC consultation is nuanced: the executive must consult the UPSC on specified matters under Article 320(3), but two things do not follow from this obligation: (1) the advice is not binding, and (2) failure to consult does not void the action taken.

• Assertion (A) is correct: Consultation with UPSC under Article 320(3) is constitutionally obligatory for enumerated matters such as disciplinary actions and promotions from one class to another.
• Reason (R) is incorrect: The Supreme Court has explicitly held that even where consultation was not undertaken, the resulting executive action is not invalidated. This is a constitutional oddity — mandatory process, non-invalidating breach.

Since A is correct and R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'mandatory consultation' and 'binding advice' is critical — the same logic applies to consultation with the Attorney General.
• The Annual Report mechanism (Article 323) serves as a partial corrective — non-acceptance of UPSC advice must be explained to Parliament.
• This principle was affirmed in multiple service jurisprudence cases before High Courts.

concepts_used: Annual Report of UPSC to the President

solution.concept_anchor: Article 323 — UPSC annual report accountability chain
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the report goes to Parliament but confuse the intermediate step (the President) may choose the sequence that omits the President entirely.
elimination_logic: The UPSC submits its annual report to the President — not directly to Parliament.
The President then places the report before both Houses of Parliament.
The memorandum explaining non-acceptance accompanies the placement before Parliament — it does not precede it.
Correct sequence: UPSC → President → Parliament (with memorandum) — option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 323 establishes the accountability mechanism for UPSC through its annual report. The report travels through a specific constitutional chain: UPSC submits to the President; the President causes it to be laid before both Houses of Parliament; if the government has not accepted UPSC's advice on any matter, a memorandum explaining the reasons for non-acceptance must accompany the report. The correct sequence is: UPSC → President → Parliament.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Places Parliament before the President, reversing the constitutional chain.
• Option (b) — Correct: UPSC to President, then President to Parliament with explanatory memorandum.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Inserts the Prime Minister's Office as an intermediate step, which has no constitutional basis here.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Suggests UPSC reports directly to both Houses simultaneously, bypassing the President.

Value Addition:
• The CAG report also goes through the President to Parliament, but via the Comptroller's audit mechanism — a parallel worth noting.
• The explanatory memorandum requirement is a key transparency mechanism — rare for a body whose advice is non-binding.
• UPSC's accountability is to the President constitutionally, not to Parliament directly.

solution.concept_anchor: President can exclude posts from UPSC purview by executive regulation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Parliament can extend UPSC functions (Article 321) may incorrectly conclude that only Parliament — not the executive — can alter the UPSC's purview.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The scenario requires action by executive regulation, not a Parliamentary law — Article 321 allows extension but not exclusion by Parliament.
Eliminate option (b): Excluding posts from UPSC purview does not require a constitutional amendment — it can be done by executive regulation under Article 320(3).
Eliminate option (c): The Union Cabinet passing a resolution is not the constitutionally prescribed mechanism — regulations made by the President are.

Confirm option (d): The President can exclude specific posts from mandatory UPSC consultation through regulations under Article 320(3) — the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958 is the operative instrument.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently over-extend the role of Parliament in UPSC matters, having learned that Parliament can expand UPSC's functions. They apply this to exclusion as well, reasoning that if expansion needs Parliament, so does exclusion. In reality, exclusion can be done by executive regulation — a deliberate asymmetry in the Constitution that the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958 operationalises.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional design of UPSC's purview contains a deliberate asymmetry: Parliament can extend UPSC's functions (Article 321), but the President can exclude specific posts and services from mandatory UPSC consultation through executive regulations under Article 320(3). This asymmetry reflects the practical need for administrative flexibility without requiring legislative amendment each time a new category of posts needs to be handled outside UPSC.

In the scenario, a ministry wishes to fill certain technical posts without UPSC involvement. The correct constitutional mechanism is for the President to issue regulations under Article 320(3) excluding those posts — as has been done through the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Parliament's role under Article 321 is to extend functions, not exclude posts.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: No constitutional amendment is needed for exclusion.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A Cabinet resolution has no constitutional backing for this purpose.
• Option (d) — Correct: Presidential regulation under Article 320(3) is the prescribed mechanism.

Value Addition:
• The UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958 has been used extensively for Group C and D posts.
• Extension of UPSC functions to Union Territories is done by Parliament under Article 321.
• The asymmetry (Parliament extends, President excludes) is a key exam-worthy constitutional design feature.

solution.concept_anchor: JPSC members appointed by President not Governor
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may identify SPSC as the odd one out because it is state-level, missing the actual distinction that JPSC members, unlike SPSC members, are appointed by the President.
elimination_logic: UPSC Chairman is appointed by the President — this is a standard constitutional provision.
SPSC Chairman is appointed by the Governor — state-level appointment.
JPSC members are appointed by the President, not the Governor — this makes JPSC different from what students might expect for a body created to serve states.
Option (c) states that JPSC members are appointed by the Governor — this is incorrect, making it the odd/wrong statement.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The JPSC trap is classic: since JPSC serves states, students assume the Governor appoints its members — analogising it with SPSC. But Article 315(2) vests the appointment power for JPSC members in the President, not any Governor. This question exploits that geographic/federal intuition.
solution.final_explanation:
A Joint Public Service Commission (JPSC) can be established by Parliament under Article 315(2) on the request of two or more state legislatures. Despite serving multiple states, the appointment of JPSC members is vested in the President — not in any Governor. This is a key distinction from State PSC members who are appointed by their respective Governors.

• Option (a) — Correctly stated: UPSC Chairman is appointed by the President.
• Option (b) — Correctly stated: SPSC Chairman is appointed by the Governor of the concerned state.
• Option (c) — INCORRECTLY stated: JPSC members are appointed by the President, NOT the Governor — this is the odd one out.
• Option (d) — Correctly stated: No JPSC currently exists in India; all states maintain their own SPSCs.

Value Addition:
• JPSC is a constitutional body created by parliamentary law — it is not directly created by the Constitution itself.
• The distinction between JPSC (President appoints) and SPSC (Governor appoints) is a recurring trap in Prelims.
• Parliament has never yet established a JPSC for any group of states since 1950.

solution.concept_anchor: Appointment — President for UPSC, Governor for SPSC

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairman and members of the Union Public Service Commission are appointed by the President without any constitutionally mandated consultation with any advisory body prior to such appointment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution requires no prior consultation for UPSC appointments — there is no provision analogous to the US Senate confirmation, nor any requirement to consult the Chief Justice or any commission before appointment.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairman of a State Public Service Commission can, after vacating office, be appointed to the Union Public Service Commission but cannot be appointed as Chairman of another State Public Service Commission.
statement_analysis.reason: An SPSC Chairman can be appointed to UPSC OR as Chairman or member of another SPSC after vacating office — the Constitution permits both options, not just one.

solution.strong_distractor: a — A student who correctly identifies statement 1 as true may assume statement 2 is also true because the restriction sounds like a reasonable constitutional design, selecting (a) without checking the exact text.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: no consultative prerequisite exists for UPSC appointments — this distinguishes India's system from presidential systems with legislative confirmation.
Statement 2 is incorrect: an SPSC Chairman CAN be appointed to another SPSC as Chairman or member — the bar applies only to the UPSC Chairman who cannot hold any further government office.
Since statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is incorrect, option (c) applies.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is crafted as a partial truth — SPSC Chairmen do have post-tenure restrictions, but the restriction in the question is more severe than what the Constitution provides. Students who know about post-retirement bars (correctly associated with the UPSC Chairman) extend it to SPSC Chairmen and assume the bar covers all future PSC appointments. In reality, SPSC Chairmen retain significant post-tenure appointment flexibility.
solution.final_explanation:
Two independent facts about appointments and post-retirement mobility in the UPSC/SPSC framework are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The President appoints UPSC members without any mandated prior consultation. Unlike the US system or judicial appointments (which involve collegium), UPSC appointments are purely executive — there is no constitutional requirement to consult anyone.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: An SPSC Chairman can be appointed as Chairman or member of the UPSC OR as Chairman/member of another SPSC. The Constitution's post-tenure bar applies strictly to the UPSC Chairman (who cannot hold any further government employment). SPSC Chairmen have greater post-tenure mobility.

Value Addition:
• The distinction in post-tenure restrictions: UPSC Chairman = absolute bar; SPSC Chairman = can go to UPSC or another SPSC.
• Removal of both UPSC and SPSC Chairmen follows the same procedure — reference to Supreme Court.
• No parliamentary confirmation for UPSC appointments is constitutionally required, unlike the CBI Director (which requires a collegium under the Lokpal Act).

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC consulted for inter-class promotions not intra-class
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know UPSC is consulted for 'promotions' broadly may select 'all promotions within and across classes,' not knowing the specific constitutional limitation to inter-class promotions only.
elimination_logic: UPSC consultation for promotions is constitutionally limited — not all promotions require it.
Routine within-class promotions are handled by Departmental Promotion Committees, not UPSC.
The constitutional requirement for UPSC consultation covers promotions from one class of service to another — i.e., inter-class promotions.
The correct completion is 'promotions from one class of service to another' — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works by offering an option that extends UPSC's consultation mandate to 'all promotions' when the Constitution limits it to inter-class promotions. Students who have a general sense that UPSC is involved in promotions but do not know the precise limitation are caught by option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
UPSC's advisory role in promotions is constitutionally circumscribed. The consultation requirement applies to promotions from one class of service to another — for example, from Group B to Group A. Routine within-class promotions (within Group A, for instance) are handled by Departmental Promotion Committees without mandatory UPSC involvement.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Extending UPSC consultation to all promotions, including within-class ones, overstates the constitutional mandate.
• Option (b) — Correct: 'Promotions from one class of service to another' accurately reflects the constitutional scope.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Limiting UPSC's role to transfers between departments omits the promotional context entirely.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Confines UPSC to only All India Services, missing the broader application to Union civil services.

Value Addition:
• DPCs (Departmental Promotion Committees) chaired by the UPSC Chairman or a member handle Group A promotions to senior posts.
• Transfers from one service to another (not just promotions) also require UPSC consultation.
• All India Services cadre management is handled by DOPT, with UPSC's role limited to initial recruitment.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) sounds constitutionally sophisticated — students familiar with Parliament's power over money bills may believe Parliament can reduce UPSC budget through that mechanism, making the 'incorrect' pairing feel plausible.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): UPSC does not report to Parliament directly — it submits its annual report to the President.
Eliminate option (c): UPSC's expenditure is charged on the CFI, so Parliament cannot reduce it through a money bill or otherwise — this pairing reverses the constitutional protection.
Eliminate option (d): Parliament cannot curtail constitutionally mandated UPSC functions — only extend them under Article 321.

solution.final_explanation:
The financial independence of UPSC is secured by charging its expenditure to the Consolidated Fund of India, which means Parliament cannot vote to reduce the UPSC budget through the regular appropriation process.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: UPSC expenditure charged on CFI → insulated from Parliamentary vote. This is accurate.

• 'Charged' expenditure cannot be put to vote — it is presented to Parliament only for discussion.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC as constitutional carve-out from doctrine of pleasure

statement_analysis.statement: The doctrine of pleasure under Article 310 of the Constitution applies to UPSC members in the same manner as it does to other government servants.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 317 creates a specific constitutional exception for UPSC members — they can be removed only on specified grounds after a Supreme Court inquiry, overriding the general doctrine of pleasure under Article 310.

statement_analysis.statement: The UPSC is classified as a constitutional body because it derives its existence, composition, and functions directly from the Constitution, not from a parliamentary statute.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC is established under Articles 315–323 of the Constitution itself — its existence does not depend on any parliamentary legislation, distinguishing it from statutory bodies like SEBI or NHRC.

statement_analysis.statement: The constitutional protection afforded to UPSC members from summary removal places them in the same institutional category as the Comptroller and Auditor General, the Chief Election Commissioner, and Supreme Court judges.
statement_analysis.reason: All these functionaries enjoy constitutional protection from arbitrary removal — through Supreme Court inquiry (UPSC), Parliamentary address (CAG, CEC, judges) — all overriding the doctrine of pleasure.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know UPSC members have removal protection may still be unsure whether it is categorically the same as the SC judges' protection (which requires Parliamentary address), leading them to doubt statement 3.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: Article 317 is a specific carve-out from Article 310 — doctrine of pleasure does not apply to UPSC members in the standard manner.
Statement 2 is correct: UPSC derives its being from Part XIV of the Constitution directly — not from any statute.
Statement 3 is correct in spirit: UPSC, CAG, CEC, and SC judges all have overriding constitutional protection from arbitrary removal, even if the exact mechanism differs slightly.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in statement 3 works by grouping UPSC members with judges whose removal requires a Parliamentary address — the mechanisms differ (SC inquiry vs. address), but the institutional category (independence from executive pleasure) is the same. Students who focus on procedural differences may wrongly reject statement 3.
solution.final_explanation:
The doctrine of pleasure (Article 310) is the general rule for government servants — they serve at the pleasure of the President. Article 317 carves UPSC members out of this general rule by specifying that removal requires both specified grounds and a Supreme Court inquiry.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The doctrine of pleasure is explicitly overridden for UPSC members by Article 317.
• Statement 2 — Correct: UPSC is a constitutional body — its source of authority is Part XIV of the Constitution, not any Act of Parliament.
• Statement 3 — Correct: While the removal mechanisms differ (SC inquiry for UPSC; Parliamentary address for CAG/CEC/judges), all these bodies are placed in the same category of independent constitutional institutions insulated from executive pleasure.

Value Addition:
• Statutory bodies like SEBI, NHRC, TRAI lack this constitutional protection — their removal can be structured by Parliament.
• The CBI Director's protection comes from the Lokpal Act, 2013 — not the Constitution directly.
• Article 310 doctrine of pleasure also does not apply to High Court and Supreme Court judges under Articles 124 and 217.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC advisory role in disciplinary matters — non-binding

statement_analysis.statement: When the UPSC tenders advice in disciplinary cases involving civil servants, it performs a quasi-judicial function to which the principles of natural justice may apply.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC's advisory role in disciplinary proceedings is recognised as having a quasi-judicial character — making natural justice principles applicable in certain procedural contexts.

statement_analysis.statement: The advice tendered by UPSC in disciplinary matters constitutes a binding decision that the executive is constitutionally obligated to implement.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC's advice is advisory and not binding — the executive retains the final decision-making authority. UPSC's advice is not a 'decision' in law.

statement_analysis.statement: Judicial review of UPSC actions in disciplinary matters can be sought before the Supreme Court under Article 32 or before High Courts under Article 226.
statement_analysis.reason: Since UPSC performs public functions with constitutional backing, both the Supreme Court and High Courts have jurisdiction to review UPSC's actions through writ jurisdiction.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who equate 'mandatory consultation' with 'binding advice' easily accept statement 2 as correct, missing the fundamental distinction between the obligation to consult and the obligation to comply.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: quasi-judicial character of UPSC in disciplinary advice is an established legal position.
Statement 3 is correct: writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 is available against UPSC actions.
Statement 2 is NOT correct: UPSC advice is advisory — the executive is not bound to implement it.
Only statement 2 is incorrect — answer is option (b) 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the confusion between mandatory consultation and binding outcomes. Students who have memorised that 'UPSC must be consulted' may leap to the conclusion that the resulting advice must be implemented, conflating procedural obligation with substantive compliance.
solution.final_explanation:
UPSC's role in disciplinary matters occupies a constitutionally unusual position: the consultation is mandatory, but the advice is not binding; and while UPSC acts in a quasi-judicial capacity, its 'advice' is not a decision subject to direct judicial review — it is the final executive order that courts review.

• Statement 1 — Correct: UPSC's disciplinary advisory function carries a quasi-judicial character, requiring procedural fairness.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: UPSC advice is explicitly non-binding. The government must explain non-acceptance in its Annual Report to Parliament, but it can validly override UPSC's recommendations.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) have jurisdiction over UPSC — however, courts typically review the executive's final order, not UPSC's advice directly.

Value Addition:
• The Annual Report mechanism under Article 323 is the primary transparency check on non-acceptance of UPSC advice.
• UPSC is not consulted for disciplinary matters involving IAS/IPS officers on state cadre — those are handled differently.
• CAT (Central Administrative Tribunal) under Article 323A also handles service matters but does not substitute UPSC's advisory role.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 318 — President's regulation-making power for UPSC service conditions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who associate rule-making for service conditions with Parliament (because Parliament legislates on civil services) may select option (b), missing that this specific power is vested in the President under Article 318.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Parliament does not make regulations under Article 318 — the President does.
Eliminate option (c): The UPSC has no self-regulatory power over its own members' service conditions.
Eliminate option (d): The Union Cabinet as a collective body is not the authority under Article 318 — it is the President.
Confirm option (a): Article 318 explicitly vests the power to regulate UPSC composition and service conditions in the President.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap here involves substituting Parliament for the President. Students who know Parliament legislates civil service rules generally may attribute Article 318 regulation-making to Parliament, especially since these regulations are later placed before Parliament — but placement before Parliament is not the same as Parliament making them.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 318 vests in the President the power to make regulations relating to the number of members of UPSC and their service conditions. A parallel power is vested in the Governor for State PSC members.

• Option (a) — Correct: The President makes regulations under Article 318 regarding UPSC composition and service conditions.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Parliament's role under Article 321 is to extend UPSC functions — not to make service condition regulations.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The UPSC has no self-regulatory authority over its own members' conditions of service.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Union Cabinet does not act as the regulatory authority here — the constitutional text names the President.

Value Addition:
• Regulations under Article 318 are placed before Parliament but are NOT subject to Parliamentary approval — merely informational.
• The Governor's parallel power under Article 318 is for State PSC regulations — placed before the State Legislature.
• This regulation-making power is distinct from the ordinary delegated legislation power under parliamentary statutes.

solution.concept_anchor: Lateral entry through UPSC — Article 320 compliance and reservation controversy

statement_analysis.statement: Lateral entry recruitment of mid-career specialists to positions like Joint Secretary through the UPSC satisfies the constitutional requirement under Article 320 for UPSC involvement in recruitment.
statement_analysis.reason: Since lateral entry recruitment is routed through the UPSC, it fulfils Article 320's mandate for UPSC's role in recruitment to civil services under the Union.

statement_analysis.statement: The reservation policy under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) does not apply to lateral entry posts because such posts are filled through a one-time selection process rather than the standard civil services pipeline.
statement_analysis.reason: The constitutional provisions on reservation (Articles 15(4) and 16(4)) do not contain an exemption for one-time or lateral entry selections — their applicability to such posts is a live constitutional controversy, not a settled exemption.

statement_analysis.statement: The allocation of cadre or service to laterally recruited officers, after UPSC selection, is a function performed by the Department of Personnel and Training, not by the UPSC itself.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC's role ends at selection — cadre assignment and allocation are administrative functions performed by DOPT, making recruitment a two-step process.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student aware of controversies around lateral entry may assume all three statements are contested or incorrect, selecting (d) — but statements 1 and 3 describe settled constitutional/administrative positions.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: routing lateral entry through UPSC satisfies Article 320 requirements — this is the government's constitutional justification for the process.
Statement 2 is incorrect: the Constitution does not carve out lateral entry posts from reservation requirements — this is an unsettled constitutional question, not a settled exemption.
Statement 3 is correct: DOPT handles cadre assignment post-UPSC selection — the two-step process is a well-established administrative practice.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial truth — it states correctly that there is no explicit reservation in lateral entry practice, but then falsely characterises this as a constitutionally valid exemption. Students aware of the controversy may accept this as a correct statement of the controversy without recognising it misrepresents the constitutional position.
solution.final_explanation:
Lateral entry recruitment into senior government positions (Joint Secretary, Director, Deputy Secretary levels) through the UPSC has been a significant policy development. Three constitutional and administrative dimensions are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The government's constitutional argument for lateral entry's validity rests on routing it through UPSC, thereby satisfying Article 320's recruitment mandate.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no constitutional exemption from reservation requirements for lateral entry posts. The question of whether SC/ST/OBC reservations apply to lateral entry posts is contested and has been subject to political and legal debate — it is not a settled exemption.
• Statement 3 — Correct: UPSC selects; DOPT allocates cadre. This two-step process applies to regular civil services as well as lateral entrants.

Value Addition:
• Lateral entry was formally announced in 2018; the first batch of lateral entrants joined as Joint Secretaries in 2019.
• The reservation controversy led the government in 2024 to cancel a lateral entry advertisement following political pressure.
• UPSC's role in lateral entry distinguishes India's system from many countries where lateral entry bypasses merit-selection bodies.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 317 — President suspends, SC recommends, President removes

statement_analysis.statement: The President of India can remove a UPSC member on grounds of misbehaviour without referring the matter to the Supreme Court, if the President is personally satisfied of the misconduct.
statement_analysis.reason: Misbehaviour is one of the grounds that mandatorily requires a Supreme Court inquiry — the President cannot act unilaterally on this ground under Article 317.

statement_analysis.statement: The President has the power to suspend a UPSC member pending an inquiry by the Supreme Court into allegations of misbehaviour.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 317 explicitly grants the President the power to suspend a UPSC member pending a Supreme Court inquiry — suspension does not require the completion of that inquiry.

statement_analysis.statement: A UPSC member can be removed by the President on the ground that the member has been adjudged insolvent, without a Supreme Court inquiry.
statement_analysis.reason: While misbehaviour requires a Supreme Court inquiry, the ground of insolvency (and certain other specified grounds) allows the President to remove a member without a Supreme Court inquiry under Article 317(3).

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court's recommendation for removal of a UPSC member following an inquiry is binding on the President.
statement_analysis.reason: When the Supreme Court recommends removal after its inquiry into misbehaviour, the President is constitutionally bound by that recommendation — this is not merely advisory.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the SC inquiry is mandatory for misbehaviour may generalise it to all grounds, rejecting statement 3 and arriving at 'only two' correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: misbehaviour requires mandatory Supreme Court inquiry — President cannot act unilaterally.
Statement 2 is correct: Presidential power to suspend pending SC inquiry is explicit in Article 317.
Statement 3 is correct: insolvency and certain other grounds do not require SC inquiry — the President can act directly.
Statement 4 is correct: SC's recommendation post-inquiry is binding on the President.
Three statements are correct (2, 3, 4) — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the key distractor — students over-generalise the Supreme Court inquiry requirement to all Article 317 grounds. In reality, the SC inquiry is required only for the misbehaviour ground; for grounds like insolvency and paid outside employment, the President can act directly. This is one of the most precisely tested distinctions in Article 317 questions.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 317 structures the removal of UPSC members through a differentiated mechanism depending on the ground of removal.

For the misbehaviour ground: a mandatory Supreme Court inquiry is required, and the President can suspend pending this inquiry. Once the SC recommends removal, the President is bound to act.

For other specified grounds (insolvency, paid employment, etc.): the President can remove directly without a Supreme Court inquiry.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Misbehaviour requires SC inquiry — unilateral Presidential action is not permitted.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Presidential suspension power pending SC inquiry is explicit.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Insolvency ground does not require SC inquiry — President may remove directly.
• Statement 4 — Correct: SC's post-inquiry recommendation is binding, not merely advisory.

Three statements (2, 3, 4) are correct — answer is (c) Only three.

Value Addition:
• The differentiated removal procedure (SC inquiry for misbehaviour; direct action for other grounds) is unique to UPSC in this form.
• Compare: CAG and Chief Election Commissioner require Parliamentary address for removal — no SC inquiry.
• Judges (SC and HC) also require Parliamentary address — not SC inquiry — making UPSC's mechanism distinct.
solution.correct_option_note: Answer should be (c) Only three — statements 2, 3, and 4 are correct.

solution.concept_anchor: JPSC — Parliament creates by law, not directly by Constitution
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. A Joint PSC is created by an Act of Parliament under Article 315(2) when two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting it.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. JPSC members are appointed by the President, not the Governor — this is constitutionally prescribed.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The Presidential appointment of JPSC members is independent of how the JPSC is created (by Parliamentary law). The reason why Parliament creates the JPSC is to serve multiple states through a single body — Presidential appointment is a consequence of its all-India character, not the cause of Parliament's creation role.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — answer is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a reversed-causation design. Students who read both A and R as correct may conclude R explains A — reasoning that 'because the President appoints members, Parliament must be the creating authority.' But the causal chain runs differently: Parliament creates the JPSC because it serves multiple states (a federal coordination rationale), and Presidential appointment follows from the same federal character. R is true but is a consequence of the same underlying rationale, not the cause of A.
solution.final_explanation:
A Joint PSC may be established under Article 315(2) when two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament to do so. Parliament then passes a law establishing the JPSC. Once established, JPSC members are appointed by the President — not by any Governor.

• Assertion (A) is correct: JPSC is created by a parliamentary law on state request — it is not directly created by the Constitution itself (unlike UPSC, which is directly constituted under Article 315).
• Reason (R) is correct: JPSC members are appointed by the President — not by the Governors of the states it serves.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The Presidential appointment of JPSC members is an independent constitutional design choice reflecting the body's multi-state character. It does not cause or explain why Parliament (rather than the states) creates the JPSC.

Answer: Both A and R correct, R does not explain A → option (b).

Value Addition:
• UPSC is directly constituted by Article 315(1); JPSC is created by Parliamentary law under Article 315(2) — a key constitutional distinction.
• No JPSC has ever been created in India since the Constitution came into force.
• The JPSC's members being appointed by the President reflects the principle that multi-state bodies require central authority coordination.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC does not cover Group C and D posts

statement_analysis.statement: The UPSC is constitutionally excluded from having any role in recruitment to Group C and Group D posts under the Union, as these are left to departmental authorities.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution (through presidential regulations under Article 320) and the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) Regulations, 1958, exclude Group C and D posts from mandatory UPSC involvement — departmental authorities handle these.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament has the authority to extend the functions of the UPSC to recruitment for Union Territories under Article 321.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 321 explicitly empowers Parliament to extend UPSC's functions to Union Territories, scheduled castes and tribes, or other purposes — Parliament has exercised this power for Union Territories.

statement_analysis.statement: The President may extend the functions of the UPSC to cover additional posts through regulations made under Article 320(3), without requiring Parliamentary legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Extension of UPSC functions requires Parliamentary legislation under Article 321; the President's regulatory power under Article 320(3) is for exclusion, not extension — this is the key asymmetry.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know the President has regulation-making power over UPSC (under Article 318) may assume this extends to expanding UPSC's functional scope, choosing (d) which includes statement 3 as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: Group C and D posts are excluded from UPSC purview through regulations — this is settled practice.
Statement 2 is correct: Article 321 explicitly gives Parliament the power to extend UPSC functions — Union Territories are one such extension.
Statement 3 is incorrect: the President can EXCLUDE posts through regulation, but EXTENSION of UPSC functions requires Parliamentary law under Article 321.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in statement 3 reverses the constitutional asymmetry: extension requires Parliament (Article 321), exclusion can be done by Presidential regulation (Article 320(3)). Students who know the President has regulatory power over UPSC matters (Article 318) may incorrectly apply this to functional extension, accepting statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The scope of UPSC's functions is shaped by a constitutional asymmetry: Parliament can extend functions (Article 321); the President can exclude posts through regulation (Article 320(3) read with Article 318). This asymmetry is one of the most exam-relevant design features of Part XIV.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Group C and D posts are excluded from UPSC purview by regulation — departmental authorities and Staff Selection Commission handle these.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Parliament has extended UPSC functions to Union Territories under Article 321.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The President cannot extend UPSC functions through regulation — extension is exclusively Parliament's domain under Article 321.

Value Addition:
• Staff Selection Commission (SSC) handles Group B (non-gazetted) and Group C posts — UPSC handles Group A and Group B (gazetted).
• The asymmetry — Parliament extends, President excludes — is a precision trap that distinguishes carefully prepared candidates.
• Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) similarly handle railway posts excluded from UPSC purview.

solution.concept_anchor: Acting Chairman appointment when UPSC Chairman post is vacant
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may select option (a) because they assume the senior-most member automatically becomes Acting Chairman before any Presidential notification — reversing the constitutional sequence.
elimination_logic: The Acting Chairman of UPSC is appointed by the President when the Chairman's post is vacant — this is a Presidential prerogative, not automatic seniority-based succession.
The correct sequence is: Vacancy arises → President identifies → President appoints Acting Chairman → Acting Chairman functions until regular appointment.
Option (a) places seniority-based assumption before Presidential appointment — incorrect.
Option (c) correctly places Presidential appointment as the operative step — confirm as correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the assumption that seniority automatically determines acting appointments in government bodies. Students familiar with acting arrangement conventions in other contexts (like Chief Justice of India) may assume the senior-most UPSC member automatically acts — but Article 316 specifically requires Presidential appointment for the Acting Chairman role.
solution.final_explanation:
When the office of UPSC Chairman falls vacant or the Chairman is unable to discharge duties due to absence or any other reason, the President appoints a member of the UPSC to act as Chairman. This is not an automatic seniority-based succession — it requires affirmative Presidential action.

Correct sequence of events:
1. Vacancy or incapacity arises in the Chairman's office.
2. President identifies and appoints a sitting UPSC member as Acting Chairman.
3. Acting Chairman discharges all functions of the Chairman.
4. Regular appointment process for a new Chairman follows.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Assumes senior-most member automatically acts — no such automatic provision exists.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Places Union Cabinet recommendation before Presidential appointment — Cabinet plays no constitutional role here.
• Option (c) — Correct: Presidential appointment of Acting Chairman is the operative constitutional step.

• This Presidential appointment for acting arrangements is distinct from the formal appointment process for a regular Chairman.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC not consulted for intra-class routine transfers
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know UPSC is consulted for 'transfers from one service to another' may over-extend this to all inter-departmental transfers, selecting option (b).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The UPSC's consultation mandate applies to specific categories — blanket approval of all transfers is not UPSC's function.

Eliminate option (b): UPSC consultation is required for transfers from one service to another — but a routine transfer of an officer within the same service class between departments does not trigger this requirement.
Eliminate option (c): The DPC handles within-class promotions, not routine geographical/departmental transfers.

Confirm option (d): The transfer described — within the same service class, between departments, on administrative grounds — does not require mandatory UPSC consultation. It is a routine administrative transfer handled by DOPT/ministry.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap works by exploiting the partial knowledge that 'UPSC is consulted for transfers.' Students who know this but do not know the precise limitation (transfers from one service to another — not routine administrative transfers within the same service class) will select option (b) or (a), failing to distinguish the constitutional trigger from everyday personnel management.
solution.final_explanation:
UPSC's consultation mandate under Article 320(3) covers specific categories: disciplinary actions, promotions from one class to another, and transfers from one service to another. Routine administrative transfers — where an officer moves between ministries or departments but remains in the same service and class — do not require UPSC consultation.

In the scenario: an IAS officer is being transferred on administrative grounds between two central government departments, remaining in the IAS. This is a routine transfer within the same service — no UPSC consultation is mandated.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: UPSC does not provide blanket approval for all transfers.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Over-extends UPSC's mandate to cover routine departmental transfers, which is not constitutionally required.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: DPCs handle promotion-related decisions, not routine transfers.
• Option (d) — Correct: The transfer is within the same service class — DOPT/ministry handles this administratively without UPSC consultation.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between 'transfer from one service to another' (UPSC mandatory) and 'routine transfer within the same service' (no UPSC requirement) is critical.
• Cadre management of All India Services is with DOPT for central deputations — UPSC is not involved in routine cadre decisions.
• State-level transfers of IAS officers are handled by state governments under cadre rules.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC not under Parliamentary control — reports to President

statement_analysis.statement: The Union Public Service Commission is not under the direct control of Parliament; its constitutional reporting obligation runs to the President, who then causes the annual report to be laid before both Houses.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 323 establishes that UPSC's annual report goes to the President, who lays it before Parliament — UPSC is not constitutionally accountable directly to Parliament.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament can, through a money bill, reduce the expenditure allocated to the Union Public Service Commission in any given financial year if it finds the Commission's performance unsatisfactory.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC's expenditure is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, which means it cannot be reduced through the money bill mechanism or any Parliamentary vote — it is placed before Parliament only for discussion.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Parliament has oversight over UPSC through the annual report mechanism may assume statement 2 is also correct, conflating 'Parliamentary accountability' with 'Parliamentary financial control.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: UPSC reports to the President — Parliamentary laying is a transparency mechanism, not direct accountability.
Statement 2 is incorrect: 'Charged' expenditure cannot be voted upon or reduced — the money bill mechanism cannot be used against CFI-charged bodies.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a plausible fabrication. Students with partial knowledge of Parliamentary finance powers may believe that if Parliament is dissatisfied with UPSC, it can express this through budget reduction — analogising with other departments. But the 'charged on CFI' protection specifically prevents this. The 'money bill' framing makes it sound constitutionally precise and sophisticated, deepening the trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Two independent facts about UPSC's relationship with Parliament are tested here.

• Statement 1 — Correct: UPSC reports to the President under Article 323. Parliament's role is downstream — the President causes the report to be laid before both Houses. UPSC is not directly under Parliamentary control, unlike ministries and departments.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: UPSC expenditure is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Charged expenditure is placed before Parliament for discussion only — Parliament cannot vote to reduce it. This protection applies equally to the CAG, Election Commission, and Supreme Court.

Value Addition:
• Bodies with CFI-charged expenditure: UPSC, CAG, Election Commission, Supreme Court (salaries of judges), CAT.
• Parliament can discuss CFI-charged expenditure but cannot vote on reducing it — a critical distinction.
• The explanatory memorandum for non-acceptance of UPSC advice is one of the few mechanisms holding the executive accountable to Parliament indirectly for UPSC matters.

solution.concept_anchor: Failure to consult UPSC does not invalidate action taken
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who equate 'mandatory consultation' with 'mandatory compliance' may choose option (b), which states that non-consultation renders the action voidable — a softer but still incorrect legal consequence.
elimination_logic: UPSC consultation is mandatory under Article 320(3) for enumerated matters.
But the Supreme Court has held that failure to consult does not invalidate or void the action taken.
The blank must be completed with a phrase indicating non-invalidating effect of non-consultation.
Only option (d) correctly states 'does not invalidate the executive action taken' — confirm as correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap extends the mandatory consultation requirement to mandatory legal consequences — students assume that if consultation is compulsory, breach must void the action. The Supreme Court's contrary interpretation is the precise constitutional knowledge tested here.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 320(3) mandates consultation with UPSC on specified matters. However, this mandatory procedural requirement is not backed by an invalidating sanction — the Supreme Court has held that executive actions taken without consulting UPSC are not rendered void or illegal.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: States that action is automatically void — the SC has held the opposite.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'Voidable at the discretion of the court' is also incorrect — courts do not routinely quash on this ground.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 'Requires Presidential ratification to be valid' has no constitutional basis.
• Option (d) — Correct: Failure to consult UPSC 'does not invalidate the executive action taken' — this is the Supreme Court's established interpretation.

Value Addition:
• The non-invalidation principle distinguishes UPSC's mandatory consultation from other mandatory processes (like Article 21 due process) where breach does void the act.
• The Annual Report accountability mechanism compensates for this — non-acceptance must be explained to Parliament.
• This principle has been consistently applied in service jurisprudence by High Courts as well.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 317 as carve-out from Article 310 doctrine of pleasure
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) correctly identifies the doctrine of pleasure but incorrectly states that UPSC members require a Parliamentary address for removal — conflating the process with that of CAG and CEC, making it sound authoritative.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): The doctrine of pleasure is found in Article 310, not Article 312 (which deals with All India Services).
Eliminate option (c): UPSC members are removed after a Supreme Court inquiry, not through a Parliamentary address — that is the mechanism for CAG and CEC.
Eliminate option (d): Article 317 does not remove the doctrine of pleasure for all constitutional functionaries — it creates a specific exception only for UPSC members.

Confirm option (a): The doctrine of pleasure under Article 310 applies to government servants generally; Article 317 creates a specific exception for UPSC members, requiring removal only on specified grounds through a Supreme Court inquiry.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) is the primary conflation trap — it combines accurate knowledge about the doctrine of pleasure and UPSC's protection with the wrong removal mechanism (Parliamentary address instead of Supreme Court inquiry). Students who know UPSC members have special protection but blur the mechanism with CAG/CEC will select option (c) confidently.
solution.final_explanation:
The doctrine of pleasure under Article 310 establishes the general principle that civil servants hold office at the pleasure of the President. Article 317 creates a carve-out for UPSC members — they can only be removed on specified grounds after a Supreme Court inquiry.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Article 310 establishes the doctrine of pleasure for government servants; Article 317 creates an exception for UPSC members requiring SC inquiry for removal.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Article 310 is the correct home of the doctrine of pleasure, not Article 312 (which is about All India Services).
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: UPSC members require a Supreme Court inquiry for removal, not a Parliamentary address. Parliamentary address is the mechanism for CAG and Chief Election Commissioner.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: Article 317 creates an exception only for UPSC members — it does not modify the doctrine of pleasure for all constitutional functionaries.

Value Addition:
• Parliamentary address removal: CAG (Article 148), CEC (Article 324) — two-thirds majority required.
• Supreme Court inquiry removal: UPSC members (Article 317).
• Judicial address: High Court and Supreme Court judges — most stringent process under Articles 217 and 124.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC appointment — President without mandatory consultation

statement_analysis.statement: The appointment of the Chairman and members of the UPSC by the President is subject to confirmation by a Parliamentary committee before taking effect.
statement_analysis.reason: No parliamentary confirmation is required for UPSC appointments — this is a purely executive function of the President, in contrast with systems like the US where Senate confirmation is required.

statement_analysis.statement: The removal of the Chairman and members of the UPSC follows a process that is more stringent than their appointment, requiring mandatory judicial inquiry rather than executive action alone.
statement_analysis.reason: While appointment is purely executive (by the President without consultation), removal requires a Supreme Court inquiry for the misbehaviour ground — making removal a quasi-judicial process more stringent than appointment.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chairman of a State Public Service Commission is appointed by the Governor of the respective state, while members of a Joint Public Service Commission are appointed by the President.
statement_analysis.reason: SPSC Chairman is appointed by the Governor; JPSC members are appointed by the President (not the Governors of the concerned states) — these are distinct constitutional provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who are aware of various consultative appointments (like collegium for judges) may assume Parliament or some body must confirm UPSC appointments, making statement 1 seem plausible and pushing them toward option (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is incorrect: no Parliamentary confirmation process exists for UPSC appointments — this distinguishes India from the US model.
Statement 2 is correct: removal requires SC inquiry (for misbehaviour), making it more procedurally stringent than the purely executive appointment.
Statement 3 is correct: SPSC = Governor appoints; JPSC members = President appoints — the asymmetry is constitutionally clear.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is an entity-swap fabrication that sounds plausible — many democracies require legislative confirmation for key appointments. Students who apply comparative constitutional knowledge from other systems (particularly the US) may accept statement 1 as accurate for India.
solution.final_explanation:
Three dimensions of UPSC appointment are tested: parliamentary confirmation (absent), asymmetry between appointment and removal, and the SPSC vs. JPSC distinction.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: UPSC appointments are purely presidential — no Parliamentary confirmation, collegium, or advisory body is constitutionally mandated. India deliberately chose executive appointment without legislative veto.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The appointment-removal asymmetry is constitutionally significant. Appointment is done by the President alone; removal requires either direct action (for insolvency/other grounds) or a Supreme Court inquiry (for misbehaviour) — the latter being significantly more stringent.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Governor appoints SPSC Chairman; President appoints JPSC members — a distinction that catches candidates who assume JPSC appointment follows state-level logic.

Value Addition:
• The contrast with the US Senate's advice and consent for executive nominations is a useful comparative anchor.
• CBI Director appointment involves a collegium (Lokpal Act) — unlike UPSC, where no such mechanism is constitutionally required.
• JPSC's Presidential appointment reflects its federal character — it serves multiple states and falls under Union coordination.

concepts_used: Regulation-Making Power Concerning UPSC

solution.concept_anchor: Article 318 regulations — placed before Parliament but not subject to approval
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The President makes regulations under Article 318 regarding UPSC composition and service conditions, and these regulations are placed before Parliament.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Regulations under Article 318 are placed before Parliament only for information and discussion — they are NOT subject to Parliamentary approval, modification, or annulment.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The fact that regulations are not subject to Parliamentary approval does not cause or explain why the President makes them (the President's regulatory power flows from Article 318 itself). R states the effect of placement, not the reason for Presidential regulatory power.
Both A and R are correct but R does not causally explain A — answer is option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 318 vests the President with the power to make regulations about UPSC's composition and members' service conditions. These regulations must be placed before Parliament, but this is a transparency measure — Parliament cannot approve, disapprove, or modify them. This contrasts with subordinate legislation under parliamentary statutes, which may be subject to 'laying' procedures that allow Parliamentary annulment.

• Assertion (A) is correct: President makes regulations under Article 318; they are placed before Parliament.
• Reason (R) is correct: Parliament cannot approve or reject these regulations — they are merely informational.
• Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The President's power to make these regulations flows from Article 318 itself — not from the fact that Parliament cannot amend them. R describes the consequence of placing them, not the reason for the regulatory authority.

Answer: Both A and R correct, R does not explain A → option (b).

Value Addition:
• Similar 'place before Parliament without approval' provisions exist for presidential orders under Article 356 (President's Rule proclamation extension).
• The contrast with 'negative laying' (Parliament can annul by resolution) is exam-relevant — Article 318 regulations do not permit even negative laying.
• Governor makes analogous regulations for State PSC under the same article — placed before the State Legislature.

solution.concept_anchor: UPSC constitutional vs statutory distinction — and JPSC status

statement_analysis.statement: The Union Public Service Commission is established directly by the Constitution under Article 315(1) and does not require any parliamentary legislation for its existence.
statement_analysis.reason: UPSC derives its existence from Article 315(1) of the Constitution — it is a direct constitutional creation, not a body established by statute.

statement_analysis.statement: A State Public Service Commission is established directly by the Constitution for each state under Article 315(1).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 315(1) provides for the establishment of a Public Service Commission for each state as well — SPSCs are also directly constitutional bodies.

statement_analysis.statement: A Joint Public Service Commission, when created, has the same constitutional status as the UPSC because it is established under the same Article 315.
statement_analysis.reason: While both appear in Article 315, UPSC and SPSC are directly constituted, whereas JPSC comes into existence only through a Parliamentary law passed under Article 315(2) — making it a constitutional body created by statute, not directly by the Constitution itself.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike statutory bodies such as the National Human Rights Commission, the UPSC cannot be abolished or its core functions curtailed by ordinary parliamentary legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Being a direct constitutional creation, UPSC can only be modified or abolished through a constitutional amendment — ordinary legislation cannot displace its constitutionally mandated functions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — A student who reads 'Article 315' as the basis for both UPSC and JPSC may conclude all three of the first three statements are correct (three correct), missing the nuance that JPSC requires a parliamentary law.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct: UPSC exists directly by virtue of Article 315(1) — no statute needed.
Statement 2 is correct: SPSCs are also directly constituted under Article 315(1).
Statement 3 is incorrect: JPSC, while authorized under Article 315, requires a Parliamentary law to come into existence — it has a lower constitutional status than UPSC or SPSC.
Statement 4 is correct: UPSC's core functions cannot be abolished by ordinary legislation — a constitutional amendment is required.
Three statements are correct (1, 2, 4) — answer is (c) Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in statement 3 merges two things that appear under the same Article (315) but have distinct constitutional pathways. Students who see 'Article 315' and 'constitutional body' together may accept statement 3 without distinguishing between direct constitutional creation (UPSC, SPSC) and parliamentary law under constitutional authorization (JPSC).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 315 is the constitutional home for all public service commissions — but the pathway to existence differs by type.

• Statement 1 — Correct: UPSC is directly constituted by Article 315(1) — no Parliamentary legislation needed.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Each state's PSC is also directly constituted under Article 315(1).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: JPSC, despite being authorized under Article 315(2), comes into existence only through an Act of Parliament passed on state legislatures' request — it is a constitutional body created by statute, giving it a slightly different constitutional footing.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Statutory bodies like NHRC can be modified/abolished by ordinary law; UPSC requires a constitutional amendment — this is the key distinction between constitutional and statutory bodies.

Three statements correct (1, 2, 4) — answer is (c) Only three.

Value Addition:
• 'Constitutional body created by statute' (JPSC) vs. 'directly constitutional body' (UPSC, SPSC) is a subtle but exam-important distinction.
• NHRC, SEBI, TRAI are statutory bodies — their functions can be altered by Parliament without constitutional amendment.
• No JPSC has been created since 1950 — the provision in Article 315(2) has remained dormant.
